name: Sranan
catalog_citation: Winford, Donald & Plag, Ingo. 2013. Survey chapter: Sranan. In: Michaelis, Maurer, Haspelmath & Huber (eds.), Atlas of Pidgin and Creole Language Structures Online (APiCS Online), apics-online.info/surveys/2. Corroborating: Wilner, John (ed.). 2007. Wortubuku…
catalog_locator: APiCS survey ch. 2, Section 3 'Phonology', final paragraph (online chapter, unpaginated); Wilner 2007 Introduction p.5
catalog_quote: Syllable structure is severely constrained, with only nasals as possible word-final codas. ... the language is generally not tonal (but see Smith & Adamson 2006 on some potentially pertinent phenomena). Word stress is assigned from the right; it normally falls on the ultimate syllable if heavy (i.e. if ending in a nasal), and on the penultimate syllable if the final syllable is light (e.g. Sranán [sra ˈnaŋ] ‘Suriname, Sranan’, bikási ‘because’).

audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding APiCS quotation is verbatim at the stated place in the held file; the corroborating Wilner 2007 sentence is verbatim but on p.6, not p.5 (fix locator). The two held sources are independent (APiCS expert sketch 2013; SIL dictionary introduction 2007) and state the same right-edge rule with the same hedge (final if nasal-closed, else penult, 'normally'), so nothing suggests the weight-hedged coding is wrong. A tally of the 32 stress-marked pronunciation fields in the held Wilner dictionary shows irregular stress handled item-by-item (e.g. mamanten ['m.an teng] penult despite final nasal; fosten [fos 'teng] regular), consistent with a default rule plus lexical exceptions. sources.quote: Discusses how English stressed monosyllables surface as Sranan disyllables with an open final syllable (anaptyctic vowel), noting nasal codas as the exception to the no-coda restriction; says nothing about where word stress falls in modern Sranan.
